Senses.Explanation: Literally, to 'go along walking' or 'walk about.' The term occurs 1,022 times in 273 allowed texts and names an observable bodily action. A late biography makes the direction explicit: at night a recluse goes outside the crag to walk about, the visiting master follows, and 'each walks east and west' (隱者出巖外經行，師亦隨之，第東西各步). A Five Lamps address pairs physical condition and action: 'when well, walk about; when tired, rest' (健即經行困即歇). The same collection records Layman Feng Ji walking about the teaching hall with Foyan when a child recites a line, and records another monk 'walking under the pines one evening' when he hears a mountain spring (一夕，松下經行，聞巖泉聲). In the collected old cases, Sudhana searches in all four directions for seven days and finds Meghashri 'walking slowly on another peak' (在別峰上徐步經行). Daily timing is also explicit: a biography says a monk ate only after serving the assembly, while Bingseng watched him 'walk about after each meal' (每飯罷經行時). The term is frequently coordinated with sitting and lying as one of the body's recorded activities. These places, times, directions, companions, and contrasts support the plain action word.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched; no stable nominal self-definition was found. Distinct deployment shapes retained are walking east-west at night, walking when well versus resting when tired, walking with another person in a hall, walking under pines, slow walking on another peak, and walking after a meal. The entry adds no special category beyond what the people in the records physically do.

Senses.PreferredTarget: having sought the mind, I could not find it
AlternateTargets: I searched for the mind and could not find it at all
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘having sought the mind, it was altogether unobtainable.’ The phrase occurs 90 times in 48 allowlisted texts and belongs to the Bodhidharma–Huike exchange. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma says, ‘bring the mind and I will set it at ease’; Huike answers with this phrase; Bodhidharma replies, ‘I have finished setting your mind at ease.’ Later masters quote the line, ask why Huike answered only this rather than offering other responses, contrast it with claims by later students to say the same words, and press its grammar: if it is altogether unobtainable, ‘what is there to regulate?’ The corpus thereby uses Huike's sentence as a repeatedly examined lineage case, not as a general dictionary proposition about mind.
Senses.Note: The deviation is the promotion of one first-person reply into the fixed hinge of the lineage's ‘setting the mind at ease’ case. Huike is a lineage patriarch and remains on the master roster; this entry defines his quoted words, not the person. No second thing appears in shortened quotations.

Occurrences.Kwic: 磨曰。將心來。與汝安。祖曰。覓心了不可得。達磨云。與汝安心竟
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The reply anchored inside the complete bring-the-mind / mind-at-ease exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如二祖豈不會作許多道理。因甚麼只答道。覓心了不可得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu asks why the Second Patriarch answered only this.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既了不可得，又調箇甚麼？」代云：「老僧近來衰耄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later comment presses the wording: if altogether unobtainable, what is being regulated?

Senses.Explanation: The word means a cat. Its most heavily transmitted Zen deployment is the public case in which the eastern and western halls fight over a cat: Nanquan lifts it and says, "if you can speak, I will not cut it; if you cannot speak, I will cut it" (道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻). The assembly does not answer and the record says he cuts it; when Zhaozhou returns, he puts a straw sandal on his head, and Nanquan says he would have saved the cat. Later teachers repeatedly ask about, title, verse, and comment on "Nanquan cuts the cat" (南泉斬貓). The same word also retains its ordinary animal use, including a cat's fixed attention while catching a mouse.
Senses.Note: Later Chan records explicitly debate the killing rather than silently resolving it. One late account says one hall cited a rule that "the bodhisattva precepts do not permit keeping cats, foxes, pigs, and dogs" (菩薩戒中不許長養貓狸豬狗), while the other wanted the cat to control mice; that speaker later calls the killing a sin. Another transmitted verdict answers the question about the case with only "it takes a Nanquan" (須是南泉始得). These are attested later deployments; this entry does not project their precept explanation backward as the early record's stated intent. The simplified spelling of “cat” (猫兒) is a separate searchable entry but not a different meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉東西兩堂爭貓兒，泉來堂內，提起貓兒云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's record gives the dispute and Nanquan's condition for sparing or cutting the cat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉斬貓兒。意旨如何。印曰。須是南泉始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later exchange asks the purport of Nanquan cutting the cat and answers, “It takes a Nanquan.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩薩戒中不許長養貓狸豬狗，放他去了罷；一個是尖酸鬼，說這兩日老鼠多，前日一釜羹被鼠糞污卻，昨日兩個老鼠走入牛角去，留他這個貓兒努起眼睛照管照管也好。

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same late speaker describes the cat as cut in two and laments its innocent death; the surrounding passage calls this killing a sin.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子見貓兒捕鼠乎？目睛不瞬，四足踞地，諸根順向，首尾一直，擬無不中。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An ordinary-animal comparison describes a cat catching a mouse, eyes unblinking and body aligned.
